title: Pre-Analysis — Core Processing Standard 2 Against the Backplane Life Evidence
abstract: Closed work order re-examining the first core processing replacement standard once backplane insertion counts became visible, concluding that continuing to fit new modules into an ageing backplane was not defensible.

sections.objective: Re-examine the first core processing replacement standard in the light of backplane connector insertion count data that only became available once the maintenance task started recording it. The question was whether the standard remained a valid destination for the two hundred and twenty aircraft that had not embodied it.
sections.findings_summary: It did not. The standard was designed to keep the delivered backplane, which was the right call in 2016 when nobody had insertion count data and opening the bay floor was the thing to avoid. By 2020 the counts were visible and a rack that has been through several module changes is at or beyond its qualified connector life. Eleven backplane-related events were recorded, all intermittent, all expensive to find and all on aircraft with high counts. Fitting new modules into that backplane is spending money to arrive at a configuration that is already at its limit. The trouble shooting procedure had reached the same conclusion independently and says so in its fault description, which is a good example of the maintenance data being ahead of the engineering position. The cooling path was a secondary finding: it was sized for the original dissipation and is wrong in both directions for the new modules.
sections.next_steps: Recommend that the standard be superseded rather than continued, and that the successor renew the backplane and the cooling path together. Cancel the retrofit bulletin once the successor bulletin is available. Retain support for the aircraft that have already embodied.

similarity_seeds: intermittent module report with no function loss
connector insertion count approaching its qualified limit

tasks.title: Extract insertion counts from the fleet maintenance record
Correlate the recorded events against the counts
Assess the cooling path against the new module dissipation

evidence.similarity_note: Surfaced by similarity on the fault description; the procedure and the modification share the module part number but the reasoning that matters is entirely textual.

expected_findings.rationale: The trouble shooting procedure states that the insertion count is the strongest predictor of an intermittent module report and instructs the engineer not to change modules on a high-count rack. That position was reached from maintenance data before any engineering assessment existed.
expected_findings.resolution: Adopt the procedure's position as the basis for superseding the standard.

evidence.similarity_note: Found by entity linking on the interface unit and rail screw part numbers the task calls out.

expected_findings.rationale: The removal task records the insertion count, which is the only reason the data exists. If the backplane is renewed the count resets and the task needs to say so, otherwise the new backplane inherits the old aircraft total.
expected_findings.resolution: Add a count reset instruction to the task, effective with the successor standard.

evidence.similarity_note: Reached from the modification to its retrofit bulletin.

expected_findings.rationale: The retrofit bulletin is the vehicle by which unmodified aircraft would arrive at a configuration this work order has concluded is not defensible. It cannot remain open once a successor exists.
expected_findings.resolution: Cancel the bulletin when the successor bulletin is issued, with kit conversion at no charge.

type_data.conclusion: Closed. The standard should be superseded; the successor must renew the backplane and the cooling path together.
